title: Dietary Patterns Are Not Consistently Associated with Variability in Blood Lead Concentrations in Pregnant British Women.
ehr_evidence: The primary source of data collection was self-completed questionnaires sent to the mother. Blood samples were collected by midwives during pregnancy.
summary: Observational analysis of the ALSPAC birth cohort evaluating associations between maternal dietary patterns/food groups and blood lead concentrations during pregnancy.
key_findings: Negative association between the 'confectionery' dietary pattern and likelihood of B-Pb ≥5 µg/dL (OR: 0.62; 95% CI: 0.41, 0.94).
Positive association between 'all leafy green and green vegetables' consumption and likelihood of B-Pb ≥5 µg/dL (OR: 1.45; 95% CI: 1.04, 2.01).
Negative association between 'cakes and biscuits' consumption and likelihood of B-Pb ≥5 µg/dL (OR: 0.63; 95% CI: 0.43, 0.93).

After multiple imputation, a positive association was found for the 'healthy' diet pattern (OR: 1.58; 95% CI: 1.27, 1.97) and a negative association for milk consumption (OR: 0.77; 95% CI: 0.61, 0.98).
No significant associations were found for other dietary patterns or food groups in adjusted models.
captured_features: Dietary pattern scores derived from FFQ
study_design: Prospective birth cohort study with cross-sectional dietary and biomarker analysis
population: Pregnant British women (ALSPAC cohort), n=2167 complete cases
limitations: Temporal mismatch between first-trimester blood sampling and third-trimester dietary data collection
Self-reported dietary data subject to misreporting
Selection bias due to subsample characteristics
Inconsistency between complete-case and multiple-imputation results
